title: The law of large numbers as consistency of the mean
dek: Ȳ_n converges in probability to μ. That is the mean settling, not a bell. The CLT is a different claim about √n fluctuations once a variance exists.
story: The weak law of large numbers is a consistency statement about averages. If Y₁, …, Yₙ are iid with finite mean μ, then Ȳ_n →p μ: for every fixed ε > 0, P(|Ȳ_n − μ| > ε) → 0 as n grows. The sample mean eventually sits near the thing it estimates. The theorem does not say that a histogram of the Yᵢ becomes a bell, and it does not by itself licence a 1.96 se interval.

The central limit theorem is the next-order object. After you zoom the error by √n, the leftover fluctuation looks Normal when a variance is finite. You can have an LLN when that zoomed error is not Normal (infinite variance, other stable limits). You can also have a pretty mound of Ȳ at n = 30 and still fail the scientific ε you care about: Chebyshev only gives P(|Ȳ − μ| ≥ ε) ≤ σ²/(nε²), which is slow if σ is large or ε is tight.

In a TB QC lab a running mean of log₁₀ CFU for a stock strain should settle toward the process mean as plates accumulate. Each Tuesday plate keeps the parent scatter. Publishing one plate as “the titre” refuses the LLN. Publishing a Normal interval around a mean of n = 4 as if the titre had Gaussianised confuses the LLN with the CLT — the Normal-and-CLT plate is that second claim.
deepTitle: What settles, how fast, and what never had a mean
deep: Weak versus strong: WLLN is convergence in probability. The strong law (SLLN) is Ȳ_n → μ almost surely, under a finite-mean iid model (Kolmogorov). For lab reporting the distinction rarely changes the sentence; both are consistency, not a shape.

Chebyshev proof of the WLLN when Var(Y) = σ² < ∞: Var(Ȳ) = σ²/n, so P(|Ȳ − μ| ≥ ε) ≤ σ²/(nε²). Finite variance is a convenience for this bound, not the most general WLLN (Khintchine needs only a finite mean).

No mean, no LLN. A Cauchy parent has no expectation; the sample mean has the same Cauchy law at every n and does not settle. Heavy tails with a mean but no variance can still be consistent while refusing a classical CLT.
Bernoulli special case: Ȳ_n = π̂ →p π. That is why a prevalence estimator is consistent. The se √(π(1−π)/n) and the Normal interval are CLT/Wald objects, not the LLN.
“n > 30” is not in the theorem. Name ε, name a tail bound or a sampling law, and name whether you needed consistency or a Normal approximation.

formulas.label: Weak law (iid, finite mean)
formulas.note: For every ε > 0, P(|Ȳ_n − μ| > ε) → 0. Consistency of the mean, not a Normal shape.

formulas.label: Chebyshev on the mean (finite variance)
formulas.note: Gives a rate. Loose if tails are light; honest if you refuse a shape.

visual.caption: Same parent, three laws: the wide law of Y, the still-wide sampling law of Ȳ at small n, and the tight mound of Ȳ at large n sitting on μ. The LLN is that last mound collapsing onto the mean — not a claim that any of the three curves is Gaussian.

example.title: A titre mean that settles, and one that only looks Normal
example.setup: QC strain, iid log₁₀ CFU with μ = 6.0 and σ = 0.4. First: n = 4 plates. Second: n = 100. Someone quotes both means as “the titre, Gaussian by CLT.”

steps.title: What the LLN promised
steps.body: Both Ȳ_n are consistent for 6.0 as n grows. At n = 4, Chebyshev with ε = 0.2 gives P(|Ȳ − 6| ≥ 0.2) ≤ 0.16 / (4 × 0.04) = 1, a vacuous bound: you have not yet bought a useful ε at this n.

steps.title: n = 100
steps.body: The same ε = 0.2 now has Chebyshev bound 0.16 / (100 × 0.04) = 0.04. The running mean is allowed to be called settled for this coarse ε. The parent plates are still σ = 0.4 wide.

steps.title: What the CLT would add
steps.body: A Normal approximation for Ȳ uses se = 0.4/√n. That is a shape-and-interval claim. The LLN only said the mass around μ piles up. Do not print 1.96 se because “the mean converged.”

example.takeaway: The LLN is consistency of Ȳ. Speed and Gaussian intervals are extra theorems.

check.prompt: The classical weak law of large numbers is a statement that:
choices: The histogram of the raw Yᵢ becomes Normal once n exceeds 30
The sample mean Ȳ_n converges in probability to E[Y], given a finite mean
√n (Ȳ_n − μ) is exactly N(0,1) at every finite n
check.answer: The sample mean Ȳ_n converges in probability to E[Y], given a finite mean
check.why: That is consistency of the mean. Shape of Y, and Normal limits after √n zoom, are different claims.

whyWrong.The histogram of the raw Yᵢ becomes Norm: The parent can stay skewed; n > 30 is folklore, not the LLN.
whyWrong.√n (Ȳ_n − μ) is exactly N(0,1) at every: That is a CLT-style fluctuation claim, and even the CLT is a limit, not an exact finite-n Normal.
whyWrong.Variance must be infinite: A finite mean is the usual ingredient; infinite variance can still allow an LLN while breaking the classical CLT.

check.prompt: iid Y with σ = 2, n = 100, ε = 1. Chebyshev’s bound on P(|Ȳ − μ| ≥ 1) is:
check.why: σ²/(nε²) = 4 / (100 × 1) = 0.04. The bound is on the mean’s deviation, not on one Y.

whyWrong.1: That would be a vacuous probability bound, here the arithmetic is 4/100.
whyWrong.0.02: That is 2/100, using σ instead of σ² in the numerator.
whyWrong.4: That is σ², not the probability bound.

check.prompt: On the density plate, the narrowest curve is Ȳ at large n in order to show:
check.figureHint: Three curves: parent Y, Ȳ small n, Ȳ large n.
choices: That the parent Y has become Gaussian
That the sampling law of the mean concentrates around μ as n grows — the LLN picture
That variance of Ȳ grows with n
check.answer: That the sampling law of the mean concentrates around μ as n grows — the LLN picture
check.why: The parent stays wide. Concentration of Ȳ is the consistency claim.

whyWrong.That the parent Y has become Gaussian: The wide parent is still drawn; Gaussianity is not the LLN.
whyWrong.That Cauchy means settle fastest: Cauchy has no mean; the sample mean does not settle.
